title: Writing formulae of ionic compounds
keyIdea: An ionic compound has no overall charge, so the positive and negative charges in its formula must add to zero. Use the lowest whole-number ratio of ions that does this: Mg²⁺ with Cl⁻ needs two chloride ions (MgCl₂), and Al³⁺ with O²⁻ needs the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2, which is 6, so two Al³⁺ and three O²⁻ (Al₂O₃). Compound ions such as hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻ and ammonium NH₄⁺ stay together, and need brackets when there is more than one: Ca(OH)₂. A Roman numeral gives a metal's charge: iron(III) is Fe³⁺.
familyTip: Read the labels on household products together, such as sodium chloride (salt), calcium carbonate (chalk or antacids) or magnesium sulfate (bath salts). Ask your teenager to say which ions are inside and check that the charges cancel.

visual.caption: Is the formula correct, or does it break a rule? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: add ions until the + and − charge bars match, then build compounds from their names and spot broken formulae.

kid: An ionic compound is made of ions. The positive ions come from a metal. The negative ions come from a non-metal. The compound has no charge overall, so the plus and minus charges must cancel.
Mg²⁺ has a charge of +2. Cl⁻ has a charge of −1. One Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ to cancel. So the formula is MgCl₂. The small 2 tells you there are two chloride ions.
Some pairs need a bit more work. Al³⁺ is +3 and O²⁻ is −2. Find the smallest number both go into: 6. Two Al³⁺ make +6. Three O²⁻ make −6. So you write Al₂O₃. Always use the smallest whole numbers.
Some ions are a group of atoms, like OH⁻. Keep the group together. If you need two, put brackets round it: Ca(OH)₂. A Roman numeral gives the charge on the metal: iron(III) is Fe³⁺.
adult: Ages 14 to 16. AQA GCSE Chemistry (4.2.1.3 ionic compounds and 4.2.1.5 formulae) expects students to work out the charge on ions from the group number and to write formulae of ionic compounds from the charges, including compound ions. The KS3 programme of study introduces chemical symbols and formulae. NGSS HS-PS1-1 asks students to use the periodic table to predict how atoms combine.

The method is to write both ions with their charges and then find the lowest common multiple of the charge sizes. Divide it by each charge to get the number of each ion, and write those as subscripts after the ion, leaving out 1. Compound ions such as hydroxide, nitrate, carbonate, sulfate and ammonium are treated as single units, so a subscript after a bracket multiplies every atom inside. The formula shows the simplest ratio of ions in a giant lattice, not a molecule.

Common mistakes: writing ions one to one whatever the charges (MgCl, AlO); putting the numbers on the wrong ions (Al₃O₂, which gives +9 and −4); leaving out brackets, so CaOH₂ seems to have one oxygen and two hydrogens; not simplifying (Mg₂O₂ instead of MgO); and ignoring a Roman numeral, which gives the metal's charge. The 'swap and drop' shortcut gives the right answer only if students then simplify, so the lab shows why it works with charge bars.

practice.prompt: Sodium forms Na⁺ and oxygen forms O²⁻. What is the formula of sodium oxide?
practice.hint: One O²⁻ is −2. How many Na⁺ make +2?
practice.explain: Two Na⁺ (+2) cancel one O²⁻ (−2), so the formula is Na₂O. NaO has a total charge of −1, and NaO₂ has −3.

practice.prompt: What is the total positive charge on {n} aluminium ions, Al³⁺?
practice.hint: Each Al³⁺ carries +3, so multiply by the number of ions.
practice.explain: {n} × (+3) = +{=3*n}. The negative ions in the compound must add up to −{=3*n}.

practice.prompt: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. How many sodium ions, Na⁺, balance {n} sulfate ions?
practice.hint: Each sulfate is −2. Each sodium ion is +1.
practice.explain: {n} sulfate ions carry −{=2*n}, so you need {=2*n} Na⁺. One sulfate needs two Na⁺, which is why sodium sulfate is Na₂SO₄.

practice.prompt: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻. What is the formula of calcium nitrate?
practice.hint: You need two nitrate ions. How do you show two of a group of atoms?
practice.explain: Ca²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻, and the brackets show two whole nitrate ions: Ca(NO₃)₂. CaNO₃₂ would mean 32 oxygen atoms, and CaNO₃ leaves a +1 charge.

practice.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit of Al₂(SO₄)₃?
practice.hint: The 3 after the bracket multiplies everything inside it.
practice.explain: Each SO₄ has 4 oxygen atoms and there are 3 of them: 3 × 4 = 12. Reading only the 4 forgets the bracket.

pool.prompt: Potassium forms K⁺ and sulfur forms S²⁻. What is the formula of potassium sulfide?
pool.hint: How many +1 ions cancel one −2 ion?
pool.explain: Two K⁺ make +2 and cancel one S²⁻, so it is K₂S.

pool.prompt: What is the formula of iron(III) oxide?
pool.hint: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺. Oxide is O²⁻. Use the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2.
pool.explain: 6 is the lowest common multiple: two Fe³⁺ make +6 and three O²⁻ make −6, so Fe₂O₃. FeO is iron(II) oxide, and Fe₃O₂ puts the numbers on the wrong ions.

pool.prompt: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of ammonium sulfate?
pool.hint: Two ammonium ions are needed. Keep each one together.
pool.explain: Two NH₄⁺ (+2) cancel one SO₄²⁻ (−2). Brackets show two whole ammonium ions: (NH₄)₂SO₄.

pool.prompt: How many hydroxide ions, OH⁻, balance {n} magnesium ions, Mg²⁺?
pool.hint: Each Mg²⁺ is +2 and each OH⁻ is −1.
pool.explain: {n} × (+2) = +{=2*n}, so {=2*n} OH⁻ are needed. That is why magnesium hydroxide is Mg(OH)₂.

pool.prompt: Why is MgCl the wrong formula for magnesium chloride?
pool.hint: Add the charges: Mg²⁺ and one Cl⁻.
pool.explain: +2 − 1 = +1, so MgCl is not neutral. Two Cl⁻ are needed: MgCl₂. Mg₂Cl makes it worse, with +3.

pool.prompt: Copper(II) forms Cu²⁺. What is the formula of copper(II) oxide?
pool.hint: Compare the sizes of the two charges.
pool.explain: Cu²⁺ (+2) and O²⁻ (−2) cancel one to one, so CuO. Cu₂O is copper(I) oxide, made from Cu⁺.

pool.prompt: How many oxide ions, O²⁻, are in {n} formula units of Al₂O₃?
pool.hint: Each formula unit has three O²⁻.
pool.explain: {n} × 3 = {=3*n} oxide ions, balanced by {=2*n} Al³⁺ ions.

pool.prompt: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻. Which formula is right?
pool.hint: One Mg²⁺ needs how many NO₃⁻? Do they need brackets?
pool.explain: One Mg²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻, shown with brackets: Mg(NO₃)₂. MgNO₃ leaves +1, and Mg₂NO₃ leaves +3.
